The military government of Maj. Gen. Chun Doo-hwan, which had extended martial law nationwide on 17 May 1980

content.p: In May 1980, the city of Gwangju, the capital of South Jeolla province in the southwest of South Korea, rose against a military government. For ten days, students and then ordinary residents fought paratroopers in the streets, took control of much of the city and held it for a short time before the army returned in force. The revolt was crushed on 27 May. Four decades later it is still one of the most contested episodes in South Korean history, both for the number of people killed and for who gave the orders that killed them.

The uprising grew out of the political vacuum left when President Park Chung-hee was shot dead by the head of his own intelligence service, the Korean Central Intelligence Agency, on 26 October 1979. Hopes rose for a democratic opening. Instead, Maj. Gen. Chun Doo-hwan, the head of the Army's Defense Security Command, seized control of the military in a coup on 12 December 1979, according to the Korea Herald and Korea Times.

Students kept demonstrating through the spring of 1980. On 17 May, Chun's junta extended martial law across the whole country, closed universities, banned political activity and tightened controls on the press. Gwangju News counts 95 student leaders from 55 universities detained in the capital that week. In the early hours of 18 May, Kim Dae-jung, the opposition politician from the same province, and 25 other opposition leaders were arrested, according to the Gwangju News chronology.

On 18 May, paratroopers from the 7th Airborne Brigade took up positions at Chonnam National University and Chosun University. Students who came to the campus gates were turned away and went out onto the streets instead. The Wilson Center describes the operation, ironically codenamed "Splendid Holiday", as sending two battalions of the ROK Airborne Brigade with tanks and helicopters into a city where protesters had grown to tens of thousands.

The BBC's account of the first days focuses on the way the troops fought. Paratroopers charged crowds with batons and bayonets, stripped students and other citizens to their underwear in the street and beat them, and fired into crowds. Gwangju News records that residents set fire to two police stations on 19 May, and that the first student was wounded by gunfire from troops that day. The Truth Commission later placed the first shot in front of Gwangju High School at about 4:50 p.m. on 19 May.

By 20 May, the army had cut the city's landline connections, so news of what was happening did not reach the rest of the country. The Korea Herald's own coverage was shaped by the same censorship; its 23 May issue called the events a "bloody riot" and reported that nine people had been confirmed dead. The newspaper's 2023 retrospective says that over 50 protesters were killed in a standoff on 21 May, including a pregnant woman, and that its 23 May 1980 edition did not report this.

On the evening of 20 May, drivers of taxis, buses and trucks gathered at Mudeung Stadium and drove a convoy down Geumnam-ro, the main road, carrying protesters toward the provincial office. Gwangju News says the convoy was stopped by police and troops after a standoff, and that a bus charge at a police line that night killed four officers. Later that night, troops fired on unarmed people at the Gwangju Station plaza, according to the same chronology.
content.h2: The citizen militia and the Provincial Office
content.p: The violence changed the protest. The Nation describes how, after the killings, non-student townspeople joined the revolt, and the armed resistance of Gwangju's citizen militia drove the troops back to the city's outskirts. The Nation calls the stretch of self-government that followed the Gwangju Commune, in which residents kept the city running, buried their dead and organised mutual aid.

Asia Times, in a 2016 account by a reporter who entered the city on 26 May 1980 for the Baltimore Sun, describes the militia's spokesman, Yun Sang-won, who gave a press conference at the provincial building and asked for American mediation. The reporter says the spokesman refused to give his name at the time, and said the group would "fight to the last man". Asia Times reports that fellow fighters later told the reporter that Yun had been shot in the kidney area when he came out of his office with a weapon, and that the fire that burned his body came from a grenade. These details come from survivors and family members as the reporter recorded them in 1993, not from an official record.

Troops re-entered the city early on 27 May. Asia Times says the spokesman and several holdouts were shot, and that Yun was found dead among ashes. The Nation says the army moved in on 27 May after the US commander in Korea released two divisions of Korean troops from joint command, on the strength of a White House meeting on 22 May that The Nation's reporters first described in 1996.

No single figure for the dead has been accepted by all sides, and the official numbers have changed with each review. In 1980, the government's count was about 200 dead or missing, according to the Associated Press and VOA. The Korea Times, citing the government, put the toll at 193, including 166 civilians, and a further 376 people who it says died as a result of the incident in the aftermath. Japan Times calls the official figure of 170 discredited.

The Truth Commission, created by a special law and reporting in May 2023, reconstructed the troops' movements and produced a narrower account. It found that the military fired weapons in at least twenty locations in Gwangju and South Jeolla more than fifty times in May 1980, and that 135 of the dead had died of gunshot wounds, according to Kyunghyang Shinmun. A defence ministry record listed 166 civilians dead, and the commission said more than 80 per cent of them were shot. Among the dead, it counted eight minors aged fourteen or younger and twelve women.

Injuries were counted separately. The commission counted 2,617 people hurt, using hospital and compensation files. Of the 442 people injured on 18 May, 44 later had disabilities of grade 9 or higher. The commission said many victims still carried bullets 43 years later. The Korea Times, citing a 2018 official tally, gave a lower figure of about 160 killed and 1,000 injured, and said residents believed the true numbers were two to three times higher. The two sets of figures are not reconciled, and each source says who produced its figure.

Residents, families and activists have long said that more people died than the records show. Korea Times reports that families of the dead say over 300 were killed, with dozens still unaccounted for. The BBC gave estimates of 500 to 2,000, and noted that the military was believed to have dumped some bodies in mass graves or lakes. The Truth Commission has exhumed remains in places including Yeongam, near Haenam, and the hills in front of the Gwangju Prison.
content.h2: Helicopters, orders and the question of who gave them
content.p: The commission's most contested finding concerns who ordered the troops to fire. It said statements from more than seventy people in the military's chain of command pointed to Chun Doo-hwan as responsible for the shooting, and said it would identify who was responsible. A former assistant director of human resources at Army Headquarters, quoted by Kyunghyang Shinmun, said the order to fire was not given in writing but agreed it came from Chun. Chun has denied that he ordered troops to open fire.

Helicopters are the second disputed point. A defence ministry committee reported in 2018 that the army had fired from helicopters on civilians on 21 and 27 May, and called the attacks premeditated. It could not find who ordered them, because helicopter operation logs had not been kept or could not be found. The Korea Times reported that former officers under Chun had said there were no such attacks. The 2023 commission found a 20mm bullet at Chosun University that it linked to a Cobra helicopter, which it said was the first time a bullet had been confirmed, 34 years after a former regional commander told the National Assembly the helicopter had fired there.

The Korea Times reports Chun's denials in detail. He testified in the National Assembly in December 1989 and denied responsibility. His 2017 memoir described the uprising as a riot, and he called a Catholic priest who testified about helicopter shootings a liar. Chun was on trial for defamation over those remarks when he died. The Korea Times records that he never apologised.
content.h2: The United States and the trials
content.p: The role of the United States is a separate and contested question. The Nation, whose reporters first described a White House meeting on 22 May 1980 in 1996, writes that Carter's national security team approved the use of force to retake the city and agreed to provide short-term support to Chun if he agreed to political change. Its reporters say the notes of a senior Pentagon official show that the White House knew by then that 60 people had been shot to death in Gwangju and over 400 injured. The Nation also says the US commander released two divisions of Korean troops from the joint command. The US has consistently described Gwangju as a domestic matter for South Korea. VOA reports that US officials say they lacked influence and real-time information, and that the US ambassador's team did not issue a formal apology.

After the uprising, Kim Dae-jung was arrested and sentenced to death by a military tribunal for allegedly fomenting it. The AP says that after the US intervened, his sentence was reduced and he was later freed. Chun, meanwhile, went on to become president. The military's first public version blamed Kim and then North Korean agents. The Asia Times reporter says he found evidence that the North Korean theory was a government disinformation campaign.

Chun was tried after democracy returned. Under President Kim Young-sam, he and Roh Tae-woo were convicted of mutiny and treason over the coup and the Gwangju crackdown, as well as corruption. Chun received a death sentence and Roh was given 22 and a half years. The Supreme Court reduced the sentences, and NBC reports that Chun's became life imprisonment and Roh's 17 years. Both men were released in late 1997 under a special pardon requested by President-elect Kim Dae-jung, who sought national reconciliation. The Japan Times instead says Chun was pardoned by President Kim Dae-jung; the AP and NBC do not say who signed.

Chun was also ordered to return 220 billion won, about $185 million, in the bribery case, according to Korea Times. The AP puts the sum at $190 million. Chun said he had only 290,000 won in his bank account, and more than 90 billion won remained uncollected when he died.

An apology from the state came slowly. In 2018 the defence minister, Jeong Kyeong-doo, apologised for rapes and sexual torture committed by martial law troops, after a protester said on television that she had been raped by an interrogator in 1980. The SCMP reports that the investigation confirmed 17 cases, and that victims included teenagers and a pregnant woman who was not taking part in the protests.

When President Moon Jae-in took office he ordered a reinvestigation. Speaking at the 40th anniversary ceremony in 2020, he promised the new commission would uncover those who gave the orders to open fire. The Truth Commission delivered its final report in May 2023. By then, Chun had died in November 2021, aged 90. His widow, Lee Soon-ja, apologised for the "pains and scars" caused during her husband's time in office, without naming any misdeed, NBC reports. Activists from the victims' groups said that was not enough.

The uprising remains a symbol. The BBC quoted the novelist Hwang Sok-yong, a dissident who lived in Gwangju at the time, calling it the start of the democratic movement that brought direct elections in 1987. Those elections followed mass protests, after which Chun accepted a constitutional change to allow a direct vote for president. Gwangju's victims still say that the truth of who ordered the killings is incomplete, and that the people who gave the orders have not been brought to account.
